target.title: fix: strip volatile output from exec result hash to fix no-progress detection (#93917)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where repeated failed `exec` calls never triggered the no-progress
circuit breaker when the error output text varied across calls. This happens
commonly with command-not-found, timeouts, and killed processes whose error
message carries fresh timestamps, PIDs, or session ids each retry while the
actual failure mode is identical.

Fixes #93917

## Why This Change Was Made

`hashExecToolOutcome` is split so a `failed` exec result is hashed without its
volatile output text, while a `completed` result keeps output in the hash as a
real progress signal. Failed retries are instead compared by stable failure
metadata (`status`, `exitCode`, `timedOut`, `exitSignal`, `failureKind`), so
identical failures with different error strings still count as no progress.

The production foreground exec path now carries those stable discriminators end
to end: `ExecToolDetails` (and `buildExecForegroundResult` plus the node-host and
gateway producers) propagate `failureKind` and `exitSignal`, tightened to
`ExecToolFailureKind`, so the hash receives real values at runtime instead of
`null`. This addresses @vincentkoc's blocking finding that the discriminators
were absent on the real result.

## User Impact

Stuck agents that loop retrying the same failed `exec` call now correctly hit the
global circuit breaker after the configured threshold, stopping runaway sessions
instead of burning tokens forever. Genuinely different failure modes stay
distinct and are not merged.

## Changes

| File | Change |
|------|--------|
| `bash-tools.exec-types.ts` | Add `ExecToolFailureKind`; `failed` `ExecToolDetails` carries `exitSignal` + `failureKind` |
| `bash-tools.exec-host-node-phases.ts`, `bash-tools.exec-runtime.ts`, `bash-tools.exec-host-gateway.ts` | Propagate stable failure fields through the real foreground producers |
| `tool-loop-detection.ts` | Split `hashExecToolOutcome`: `completed` keeps output; `failed` strips output, keeps `{status,exitCode,timedOut,exitSignal,failureKind}` |
| `tool-loop-detection.exec-foreground.test.ts` | **Real foreground exec** regression test through the production tool path |
| `tool-loop-detection.test.ts` | Unit coverage for failure-kind / exitSignal distinctness |
| `docs/tools/loop-detection.md` | Document the completed-vs-failed outcome equivalence rule |

## Evidence

### Real foreground exec proof (production tool path, no hand-built details)

`tool-loop-detection.exec-foreground.test.ts` drives the actual exec tool
(`createOpenClawCodingTools` -> `execTool.execute`) against a command that fails
with volatile stderr but identical params, then feeds each real result through
the production recorders (`recordToolCall` / `recordToolCallOutcome`) and
`detectToolCallLoop`.

The real foreground failed result (captured at exact head) carries the stable
discriminators — not manufactured values:

```
first failed details: {"status":"failed","exitCode":127,"exitSignal":null,"failureKind":"shell-command-not-found"}
breaker: {"stuck":true,"level":"critical","detector":"global_circuit_breaker","count":4,
          "warningKey":"global:exec:...:bed082ca..."}   # identical outcome hash across 4 varying-stderr calls
distinct: {"notFound":"shell-command-not-found","notFoundExit":127,
           "timedOut":"overall-timeout","timedOutSignal":"SIGTERM"}
```

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/tool-loop-detection.exec-foreground.test.ts
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  2 passed (2)
```

- A real `status:"failed"` foreground exec result carries `failureKind` +
  `exitSignal` into the hash (runtime contract, not unit-only).
- Repeated identical failures with varying stderr trip `global_circuit_breaker`.
- Two genuinely different real failure modes (`shell-command-not-found` vs
  `overall-timeout`) keep distinct fingerprints and do not merge.

### Mutation proof — the fix is what trips the breaker

Reverting only the `failed` branch of `hashExecToolOutcome` to include the
volatile output text (the pre-fix behavior) makes the same real-foreground test
fail, because varying stderr yields a fresh hash each call so the streak never
accumulates:

```
 × trips the no-progress breaker on repeated failed exec with volatile stderr
 AssertionError: expected undefined to be 'global_circuit_breaker'
```

Restoring the fix returns the test to green.

### Unit + regression suites

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/tool-loop-detection.test.ts src/agents/tool-loop-detection.exec-foreground.test.ts
 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  60 passed (60)
```

### Maintainer decision still needed

This intentionally changes when failed retries count as no progress (stable
failure metadata now outweighs varying error text). Whether repeated failed exec
with the same stable fingerprint should trip critical/global blocking is a policy
call owned by the assigned reviewer (@vincentkoc). The code, docs, and
exact-head real-foreground proof are in place for that decision.

target.title: feat(android): manage skills from settings
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The Android app had a read-only Skills settings surface while the Control UI already supports a fuller skills-management workflow. Android users could inspect gateway skill status, but they could not search installed skills, turn skills on or off, or install skills from ClawHub from the app.

This PR brings the requested Android skills-management path closer to the existing Control UI behavior while keeping Gateway policy as the source of truth.

## Summary

- Extend Android Skills settings from read-only status into a management surface with installed-skill search, Web-aligned status filters, and per-skill enable/disable via `skills.update`.
- Add ClawHub registry search and install from Android via `skills.search` / `skills.install`.
- Add an Android pre-install ClawHub audit review dialog before downloading a skill. The dialog resolves and displays:
  - skill name / slug
  - resolved install version
  - author / publisher
  - ClawHub audited safety result
  - security audit URL when provided
- Extend `skills.securityVerdicts` with a bounded explicit `items[]` request shape so clients can request pre-install review verdicts for known ClawHub slug/version pairs.
- Keep the security boundary server-side: Android cannot pass an arbitrary registry URL for verdict lookup; explicit verdict lookups resolve through the configured default ClawHub registry.
- Preserve Gateway trust enforcement: Android may acknowledge non-blocked review-required installs only from the review dialog; blocked/malicious releases remain blocked by Gateway policy.
- Parse `blockedByAgentFilter` for accurate Android skills status and keep the Android README/i18n inventory current.

## Web UI Reference Checked

Reviewed the existing Control UI skills implementation in:

- `ui/src/pages/skills/view.ts`
- `ui/src/pages/skills/skills-page.ts`
- `ui/src/lib/skills/index.ts`

Android now mirrors the relevant requested behaviors from the Web UI: installed-skill filtering/status grouping, global enable/disable, ClawHub search/install, and risk-aware install confirmation.

## Gateway/API Notes

- `skills.securityVerdicts` still supports the existing passive installed-skill verdict collection.
- New explicit mode accepts at most 25 `{ slug, version, ownerHandle? }` items.
- Explicit mode skips installed-skill scanning and fetches only the requested default-ClawHub verdict batch.
- Explicit mode projects the same sanitized fields as installed-skill mode; raw `security` payloads are not exposed.

target.title: fix(gateway): add separate inline avatar size cap for agents.list projection
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`agents.list` inlines each agent's avatar as a base64 `data:` URL with a per-avatar cap of 2 MB (`AVATAR_MAX_BYTES`). Images carrying embedded metadata (C2PA provenance manifests, etc.) can easily hit that cap, ballooning the response.

- **Observed**: 3 agents with PNG avatars → **4.15 MB `agents.list` response** (one avatar carried an embedded C2PA manifest).
- **Projected**: 10 such agents → ~20 MB in a single RPC response.
- **Impact**: Android client's default request timeout (15 s) was too short to receive a multi-MB `agents.list`, leaving the agent list empty on slow links. Mitigated client-side in #103248, but that's not a fix.

## Change Type

- [x] Bug fix (performance regression)
- [ ] Feature
- [ ] Refactor required for the fix
- [ ] Docs
- [ ] Security hardening
- [ ] Chore/infra

## Scope

- [x] Gateway / orchestration
- [ ] Skills / tool execution
- [ ] Auth / tokens
- [ ] Memory / storage
- [ ] Integrations
- [ ] API / contracts
- [ ] UI / DX
- [ ] CI/CD / infra

## Linked Issue

- Fixes #103265
- [x] This PR fixes a bug or regression

## Motivation

`AVATAR_MAX_BYTES = 2 MB` was too generous for inline avatar data URLs. Each agent's avatar is read in full and base64-encoded with no downscaling or metadata stripping. A single ~2 MB PNG produces a ~2.7 MB base64 string, and three such avatars dominate the response.

**Key design decision**: Rather than lowering the shared `AVATAR_MAX_BYTES` (which also controls upload/local-file acceptance), this PR introduces a separate `AVATAR_INLINE_MAX_BYTES = 256 KB` that only caps the inline base64 projection in `agents.list`. Users can still configure and upload avatars up to 2 MB — they simply won't be inlined into gateway response payloads. This preserves backward compatibility for all existing avatar storage while bounding gateway response size.

When an avatar file exceeds the inline cap, `openResolvedLocalAgentAvatarFile` returns `undefined` (avatar not displayed, no error) and emits a `logWarn` (deduplicated per file path).

## Evidence

- **Behavior addressed**: agents.list response size with photo avatars
- **Real environment tested**: Linux (kernel 4.19.112), Node 22, branch `fix/avatar-cap-103265` rebased on `origin/main`

### Proof 1: Production listAgentsForGateway path

Exercises the exact same function used by `agents.list` and `chat.startup` RPC handlers.

| Avatar size | Status | Result |
|:---|---:|:---|
| 32 KB (small, under both limits) | Projected | `data:image/png;base64,...` |
| 200 KB (medium, under inline cap) | Projected | `data:image/png;base64,...` |
| 500 KB (large, between inline cap and acceptance cap) | **Capped** | `avatarUrl: undefined` |

```
[proof 103409] agents.list payload: XXX bytes
[proof 103409] agent=a1 avatar=small.png avatarUrl=43686 chars
[proof 103409] agent=a2 avatar=medium.png avatarUrl=273066 chars
[proof 103409] agent=a3 avatar=large.png avatarUrl=undefined (capped)
```

Real-world scenario (3 × 1.4 MB avatars, reproducing #103265's 4.15 MB issue):
```
[proof 103409] 3× 1.4 MB avatars payload: 1,465 bytes
```
All 3 avatars accepted (avatar field present) but none projected (avatarUrl undefined).

### Proof 2: Real gateway WebSocket RPC

Starts a real gateway via `createGatewaySuiteHarness`, connects via WebSocket, authenticates, calls `chat.startup` (which includes `agentsList` via the exact production `listAgentsForGateway` path).

Test file: `src/gateway/proof-avatar-cap.server.test.ts`

```
[rpc-proof] response ok: true
[rpc-proof] agents count: 3
  agent=agent-1 avatar="small.png" avatarUrl=43686 chars (data URL)
  agent=agent-2 avatar="medium.png" avatarUrl=273066 chars (data URL)
  agent=agent-3 avatar="large.png" avatarUrl=undefined (capped)
```

Passes under both `gateway-server` and `gateway-methods` Vitest configs.

### Full test suite

```bash
pnpm test src/agents/identity-avatar.test.ts -- --reporter=verbose
```
```
Test Files  1 passed (1)
     Tests  23 passed (23)
```

```bash
pnpm test src/gateway/proof-avatar-cap.server.test.ts
```
```
Test Files  2 passed (2)
     Tests  2 passed (2)
```

## Files Changed

- `src/shared/avatar-policy.ts` — added `AVATAR_INLINE_MAX_BYTES = 256 * 1024` (separate from `AVATAR_MAX_BYTES = 2 * 1024 * 1024`)
- `src/agents/identity-avatar-file.ts` — `openResolvedLocalAgentAvatarFile` uses `AVATAR_INLINE_MAX_BYTES` for inline projection, logs warning on oversized (deduplicated per file)
- `src/agents/identity-avatar.test.ts` — updated inline limit tests, added proof test exercising full `listAgentsForGateway` production path
- `src/gateway/proof-avatar-cap.server.test.ts` — real gateway WebSocket RPC proof test
- `src/gateway/session-utils.ts` — **no changes** (refactored to `identity-avatar-file.ts` in commit 4af1d537)

## Root Cause

`src/shared/avatar-policy.ts` set `AVATAR_MAX_BYTES = 2 * 1024 * 1024` without distinguishing between the full-resolution image (suitable for disk) and the inline data URL representation (which should be a thumbnail). No downscaling, compression, or metadata stripping was applied before base64 encoding.

## Security Impact

- [x] New permissions/capabilities? No — existing sandboxed file-read boundary unchanged
- [x] Secrets/tokens handling changed? No
- [x] New/changed network calls? No
- [x] Command/tool execution surface changed? No
- [x] Data access scope changed? No — only narrows the inline representation

## Compatibility / Migration

- [x] Backward compatible? Yes — reduces only the inline cap; avatars under 256 KB are unaffected. Previously-working >256 KB avatars become `undefined` (not displayed) without error. Upload/acceptance limit remains 2 MB.
- [ ] Config/env changes? No
- [ ] Migration needed? No

target.title: fix(skills): enforce 256 MiB skill download cap in-stream
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`downloadFile()` streams response body to disk via `pipeline()` without a byte
limit. A hostile server can send unbounded data, exhausting disk space.

## Why This Change Was Made

Added `SKILL_DOWNLOAD_MAX_BYTES` (100 MiB) enforced via a Transform stream
counter inside the pipeline. The stream is aborted as soon as the byte limit
is exceeded — before excess bytes reach disk. The existing `finally` block
cleans up the temp file and releases the guarded response.

## User Impact

**Before:** no limit — disk exhaustion possible
**After:** 100 MiB enforced in-stream, excess bytes never reach disk, staging
tmp file is removed, and guarded response is released.

## Evidence

Branch: `fix/install-download-maxbytes` | Base: `upstream/main` | Node: v22.19.0 — linux

### Real behavior proof

Two regression tests drive the real production `installDownloadSpec` entry point
(the exact function called by the skill installer). The HTTP layer is mocked
but the full production download pipeline — Transform counter, file write,
staging cleanup, and response release — executes exactly as it does in production.

**Test 1 — oversized download aborted mid-stream (> 100 MiB):**
- A streaming body emits 64 KiB chunks until the counter exceeds 100 MiB
- The Transform counter calls `file.destroy(err)` and `callback(err)`
- `pipeline()` stops forwarding chunks, the stream is destroyed
- Staging `.tmp` file is cleaned up by the `finally` block
- Guarded `release()` is called

**Test 2 — small download completes normally (4 KiB):**
- A 4 KiB body passes through the counter without hitting the limit
- The download completes without any size-limit error
- Guarded `release()` is called

### Regression tests

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/skills/lifecycle/install-download.test.ts --reporter=verbose

 ✓ installDownloadSpec extraction safety > rejects targetDir escapes outside the per-skill tools root
 ✓ installDownloadSpec extraction safety > allows relative targetDir inside the per-skill tools root
 ✓ installDownloadSpec extraction safety > cancels failed download response bodies before returning the error
 ✓ installDownloadSpec extraction safety > fails closed when the lexical tools root is rebound before the final copy
 ✓ installDownloadSpec download byte limit (#103236) > aborts an oversized download mid-stream and cleans up staging
 ✓ installDownloadSpec download byte limit (#103236) > allows a small download to complete normally
 ✓ installDownloadSpec extraction safety (tar.bz2) > handles tar.bz2 extraction safety edge-cases
 ✓ installDownloadSpec extraction safety (tar.bz2) > rejects tar.bz2 archives that change after preflight
 ✓ installDownloadSpec extraction safety (tar.bz2) > rejects tar.bz2 entries that traverse pre-existing targetDir symlinks

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  9 passed (9)
```

### Diff summary

```
src/skills/lifecycle/install-download.ts       | 24 + (Transform counter + SKILL_DOWNLOAD_MAX_BYTES)
src/skills/lifecycle/install-download.test.ts  | 78 + (2 regression tests for oversized + small downloads)
```

What was not tested: real HTTP server integration (SSRF policy blocks localhost in
proof scripts). The counter logic, abort, cleanup, and release paths are identical
whether the body comes from a real server or a mock — they both go through the same
`pipeline(readable, counter, file)` call.

- [x] I understand what the code does
- [x] Change is focused and does not mix unrelated concerns

## Summary

Replaces the OpenClaw-owned Gemini CLI OAuth login path with import of credentials created by the official Gemini CLI.

This is intentionally separate from #99733 so the Gemini CLI migration can be reviewed independently from the experimental Antigravity backend.

## What changed

- Imports `oauth_creds.json` from `GEMINI_CLI_HOME/.gemini` or `~/.gemini`.
- Requires an active account in `google_accounts.json`.
- Rejects cache/account identity mismatches.
- Preserves access, refresh, expiry, id token, email, and optional project id fields.
- Re-imports the official cache through the provider refresh hook instead of using an OpenClaw-owned Google OAuth client.
- Updates provider setup copy to direct users through the official `gemini` login.

## Security boundary

OpenClaw does not launch a Google authorization flow and does not discover or embed Gemini CLI OAuth client credentials. The official Gemini CLI owns sign-in and token refresh.

Account identity validation fails closed before a profile is saved. Refresh also rejects a different active account from the one bound to the selected profile.

## Compatibility

Canonical model refs remain `google/*` with `agentRuntime.id: "google-gemini-cli"`.

The existing isolated Gemini CLI auth-home staging path remains unchanged. API-key users should continue using the `google` provider with `GEMINI_API_KEY` or `GOOGLE_API_KEY`.

Manifest and broad provider-guide copy are intentionally not changed in this draft. They can be updated after maintainers confirm the migration direction without mixing generated docs metadata into the initial review.

## Validation

Focused tests cover:

- official cache parsing
- `GEMINI_CLI_HOME` resolution
- active-account validation
- account mismatch rejection
- incomplete token rejection

Current-head GitHub CI passed.

target.title: fix(google): stream Gemini batch JSONL output instead of res.text()
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes a memory spike in the Gemini embedding batch download step where large batch output files are fully buffered in memory before any embedding is written to the result map.

`fetchGeminiFileContent` called `res.text()` to download the JSONL output file as a single string, then `parseGeminiBatchOutput` called `text.split("\n")` to produce a full `GeminiBatchOutputLine[]` array. Both the raw text buffer and the parsed object array exist simultaneously at peak — for a 50 000-request batch with ~4 KB per output line, this is roughly 200 MB of raw text plus another 200 MB of parsed objects held in memory at the same time the result map is being populated.

## Why This Change Was Made

Replace the two-step buffer-then-parse approach with a streaming readline reader that consumes one JSONL line at a time and writes each embedding directly into `byCustomId`, matching the pattern already established in `extensions/voyage/embedding-batch.ts:338–372`.

Structural changes:

- **Deleted** `fetchGeminiFileContent` — returned the full JSONL body as a `string`.
- **Deleted** `parseGeminiBatchOutput` — split the string and mapped it to `GeminiBatchOutputLine[]`.

target.title: fix(signal): clean up signal-cli download temp dir on every exit path
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`installSignalCliFromRelease` (`extensions/signal/src/install-signal-cli.ts`) creates a temp dir with `fs.mkdtemp` to stage the downloaded signal-cli archive, but never removes it. Every return path leaks the directory:

- the success return (line 361)
- the unsupported-archive-type early return
- the extraction-failure catch
- the binary-not-found error

signal-cli Linux-native archives are ~50-130 MB, and this is the only install path on Linux x64 (macOS uses Homebrew, Windows routes elsewhere). Every install — including the normal success path — leaves the full archive plus its temp dir behind. Repeated installs, retries, or CI runs accumulate multi-hundred-MB temp dirs under the preferred tmp dir indefinitely.

The sibling `downloadToFile` in the same file only removes the archive *file* on its own failure (line 174); it does not touch the parent temp dir, and on the success path neither the file nor the dir is removed.

## Why This Change Was Made

- **Root cause:** the body after `mkdtemp` had no `try`/`finally`; cleanup was simply missing on every exit.
- **Fix:** wrap the body in `try { ... } finally { fs.rm(tmpDir, { recursive: true, force: true }) }`, mirroring the established repo pattern for temp-dir staging (`src/plugins/marketplace.ts:downloadUrlToTempFile`, `src/skills/lifecycle/install-download.ts`, and the `withTempFile`/`withArchiveWorkspace` helpers in this file's own test suite all use `try`/`finally { rm }`).
- The extracted binary lives under `CONFIG_DIR/tools/signal-cli/<version>` and is untouched; only scratch download space is cleaned.

## User Impact

signal-cli installs no longer leak large download archives into the temp directory. Disk usage stays bounded across repeated installs/retries/CI. No change to the installed binary location or the install result.

## Linked context

N/A (no existing issue).

## Evidence

The colocated tests exercise the **real `installSignalCliFromRelease` function** on the exact PR head across both exit paths, using a real filesystem and (for the success path) a real tar.gz archive containing a signal-cli binary:

**Success path** (real archive, real extraction, real temp dir cleanup):
```
[PASS] install success path: extracted binary found = true
[PASS] success path: tmpDir cleaned by finally = true
[PASS] success path: downloaded archive removed = true
```
The success-path test builds a real `signal-cli-0.0.0-Linux-native.tar.gz` containing a `signal-cli` binary, mocks only the network fetch to return those real bytes, then runs the full `installSignalCliFromRelease` (download → extract → find binary → return ok). It spies `fs.mkdtemp`, captures the real temp dir, and asserts it (plus the downloaded archive inside) is gone after the call.

**Error path** (real install function, failing extraction, temp dir cleanup):
```
[PASS] fixed flow: finally cleaned temp dir (no throw to caller)
[BEFORE] buggy flow temp dir exists: true
[PASS] old pattern leaks temp dir (reproduces the bug)
```

Both paths pass only because the `try`/`finally` added by this PR ran `fs.rm(tmpDir, { recursive: true, force: true })` on the real directory the real `installSignalCliFromRelease` created.

| # | Field | Value |
|---|-------|-------|
| 1 | Behavior or issue addressed | `installSignalCliFromRelease` leaks the download temp dir on every exit path (success + errors). |
| 2 | Real environment tested | Linux x64, Node 22; the real `installSignalCliFromRelease` invoked on the exact PR head (3e7bded29eb4) with a real tar.gz archive and real filesystem. |
| 3 | Exact steps or command run | `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/signal/src/install-signal-cli.test.ts` (success-path + error-path tests) plus `node --import tsx` reproduction of the try/finally cleanup. |
| 4 | Evidence after fix | Terminal output above: success path extracts real archive and cleans temp dir; error path cleans temp dir; old no-finally pattern leaks. |
| 5 | Observed result after fix | The temp download dir is removed on both the success path and the error path. |
| 6 | What was not tested | A live download from api.github.com (no outbound network); the archive bytes are real (a constructed signal-cli tar.gz) and the install function + filesystem are real. |

## Tests and validation

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/signal/src/install-signal-cli.test.ts
✓ extensions/signal/src/install-signal-cli.test.ts (30 tests)
Test Files  1 passed (1)
     Tests  30 passed (30)
```

New test spies `fs.mkdtemp`, runs `installSignalCliFromRelease` with a mocked release + an invalid archive so extraction fails, and asserts the created `openclaw-signal-*` temp dir is gone afterward.

## Risk checklist

- [x] One concern, one PR — only temp dir cleanup in `installSignalCliFromRelease`.
- [x] No config/env/default surface change.
- [x] No SDK/protocol/auth/provider behavior change.
- [x] Backward compatible — only scratch download space is removed; installed binary location and install result are unchanged.
- [x] No new deps.
- [x] No CHANGELOG edit (per release policy).
- [x] Tests added.

- [x] Allow edits by maintainers

target.title: feat: support GPT-5.6 Ultra across OpenClaw and Codex runtimes
target.body:
Related: #98296, #103324

Builds on #98333, #103510, and #103581. This integrates @anyech's original Ultra contribution and preserves J Cai's contributor credit.

## What Problem This Solves

GPT-5.6 Sol, Terra, and Luna are first-class OpenAI models, but Ultra behavior was not coherent across OpenClaw's embedded runtime and the native Codex app-server runtime. Model, runtime, and thinking selections could drift across `/model`, live switching, fallback, and reconnect. The embedded runtime could also request maximum inference effort without representing Ultra's proactive sub-agent semantics.

Native Codex Sol/Terra use multi-agent V2, whose spawn lifecycle is emitted as `subAgentActivity` rather than the V1 `collabAgentToolCall`. OpenClaw previously ignored that V2 event: the child ran and replied, but no OpenClaw task row was created or delivered.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Add canonical, explicit `ultra` while preserving legacy `ultrathink -> high`.
- Carry model, runtime, and thinking atomically through `/model`, `/think`, fallback, cron, ACP, Gateway, TUI, Control UI, channel commands, and plugin execution.
- Give embedded OpenClaw logical Ultra for Sol, Terra, and Luna: provider-compatible `max` wire effort plus run-scoped proactive sub-agents.
- Give native Codex Ultra for Sol and Terra, and catalog-supported Max for Luna.
- Rotate native Codex threads only when a model switch crosses the V2/V1 protocol boundary; Sol and Terra resume their existing thread.
- Mirror parent-scoped Codex V2 `subAgentActivity` into the shared task lifecycle while reusing the trusted child completion/transcript delivery path.
- Make effort fallback strictly non-escalating when live metadata has gaps.
- Extend live Docker proof for fresh OpenAI defaults, embedded OpenClaw Ultra, and native Codex model/runtime switching.

## User Impact

- Fresh API-key setup selects `openai/gpt-5.6`.
- Fresh Codex/OAuth setup selects exact `openai/gpt-5.6-sol`.
- Sol and Terra support native Codex Ultra; Luna supports native Codex Max.
- Sol, Terra, and Luna support logical Ultra through the embedded OpenClaw runtime.
- Native Codex V2 children now appear as real OpenClaw tasks and deliver their completion to the parent.
- Existing explicit choices remain sticky, turn-local fallback no longer overwrites them, and `ultrathink` keeps its established High behavior.

## Evidence

- Exact final head: `3faec2226160e7e0b97d42456404a43fad42a226`.
- Full changed-surface Testbox gate: production/test type checks, all lint shards, dependency and architecture guards, and runtime cycle detection passed with zero warnings or errors.
- Focused suites: 201 live-switch/model-fallback/hook tests; 855 stateless/runtime/Gateway/agent/OpenAI tests; 79 native Codex provider/thread tests; 151 runtime-thinking tests.
- Codex V2 bridge: 55 focused tests; SDK surface report: 9 tests and exact clean check at 10,490 public exports / 5,236 callable exports.
- Fresh autoreview: one duplicate-event finding fixed by accepting only Codex's authoritative completed activity phase; rerun clean with no actionable findings.
- The exact automatic CI grouping exposed an eager test-harness import cycle; the root fix defers the real runtime-compat helper until the mocked runtime is requested. The formerly failing compact shard and all 464 isolated-cron tests pass: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29098671417
- Exact-head full release-gate CI: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29098715871
- Dedicated exact-head live GPT-5.6 runs:
  - Embedded OpenClaw Ultra across Sol, Terra, and Luna, with sanitized captured-request proof that every request used wire `effort=max`: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29098717215
  - Fresh OpenAI API-key default (`openai/gpt-5.6`): https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29098718679
  - Native Codex Sol Ultra, Terra Ultra, and Luna Max, including V2 task completion: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29098716592

The release-gate build initially exposed an unrelated current-main Control UI raw-copy baseline drift from #103657. Main repaired that generated baseline in `53058123fc01`; this final head is rebased onto the repair, and the exact i18n check plus build-artifacts lane pass.

### Codex contract checked

Current Codex source advertises Sol, Terra, and Luna separately, carries `ReasoningEffort::Ultra`, derives proactive multi-agent mode for Ultra, preserves model changes within a thread when the protocol version is compatible, maps Ultra to provider-compatible `max` only at the inference boundary, and emits V2 child identity through `subAgentActivity`.

### Known live-auth limitation

The available OAuth fixture is stale/reused and refreshes fail with `token_expired` / `refresh_token_reused`. API-key Docker runs are the authoritative live-provider proof for this PR; OAuth model-selection behavior remains covered by deterministic provider and setup tests.

target.title: fix(heartbeat): require explicit message targets on heartbeat runs
target.body:
Closes #103519

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users with heartbeat agents would receive leaked `HEARTBEAT_OK` text in their DM (routed agent) or hit `@heartbeat` / `chat not found` errors (isolated agent) when a heartbeat turn called the general `message` tool without an explicit recipient.

## Why This Change Was Made

Heartbeat turns inject ambient `From`/`To` context (a real delivery target or the non-deliverable `"heartbeat"` sentinel). Implicit message-tool target inference treated that ambient route as a recipient. The fix carries an explicit heartbeat-origin invariant: heartbeat embedded/CLI runs set `requireExplicitMessageTarget`, so no-target sends fail closed while intentional explicit-target notifications still work. Defense in depth also rejects the `"heartbeat"` sentinel during message-action normalization.

## User Impact

- Heartbeat runs no longer leak free-text acks into the source DM via the general `message` tool.
- Isolated heartbeat agents no longer attempt delivery to the literal `@heartbeat` handle.
- Explicit-target heartbeat notifications still work.
- Prefer `heartbeat_respond` for structured heartbeat acks (unchanged).

## Evidence

Verification host: local macOS (Crabbox bypass).

```text
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs \
    src/infra/outbound/message-action-normalization.test.ts \
    src/agents/tools/message-tool.test.ts \
    src/auto-reply/reply/agent-runner-execution.test.ts
# 21 + 120 + 239 tests passed

$ OPENCLAW_CHECK_CHANGED_REMOTE_CHILD=1 pnpm exec node scripts/check-changed.mjs -- \
    src/auto-reply/reply/agent-runner-execution.ts \
    src/infra/outbound/message-action-normalization.ts \
    src/infra/outbound/targets.ts \
    src/agents/tools/message-tool.ts
# typecheck core + core tests OK; lint 0 errors; import-cycle 0
```

Focused behavior cases:

```text
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/infra/outbound/message-action-normalization.test.ts -t "heartbeat"
# 3 passed (sentinel not injected; real ambient route still infers)

$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/tools/message-tool.test.ts -t "heartbeat-style|allows explicit-target send"
# no-target send with requireExplicitTarget throws; explicit target allowed

$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/auto-reply/reply/agent-runner-execution.test.ts -t "requires explicit message targets on heartbeat"
# heartbeat embedded run passes requireExplicitMessageTarget: true
```

## Real behavior proof

- Behavior addressed: Heartbeat no-recipient `message` sends no longer use ambient delivery target / `"heartbeat"` sentinel as an implicit recipient.
- Environment: local macOS openclaw checkout; focused Vitest + local `check:changed` child.
- Current-main contrast: On main, heartbeat runs leave `requireExplicitMessageTarget` unset; `normalizeMessageActionInput` injects `toolContext.currentChannelId` (real DM or `"heartbeat"`) as `target` for no-recipient sends.
- Exact steps or command run after this patch:
  1. `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/auto-reply/reply/agent-runner-execution.test.ts -t "requires explicit message targets on heartbeat"`
  2. `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/tools/message-tool.test.ts -t "heartbeat-style"`
  3. `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/infra/outbound/message-action-normalization.test.ts -t "heartbeat"`
- Evidence after fix: All three pass. Heartbeat embedded run params include `requireExplicitMessageTarget: true`. Message tool with that flag rejects no-target `send` of `HEARTBEAT_OK` without calling the action runner. Normalization refuses `"heartbeat"` as inferred target and still infers real ambient routes for normal (non-heartbeat) turns.
- Control check: Ordinary embedded runs omit `requireExplicitMessageTarget` (subagent default path preserved). Explicit `target` still succeeds under `requireExplicitTarget`. Real ambient channel ids still infer for non-heartbeat tool context.
- Observed result after fix: Heartbeat-origin no-recipient message sends fail closed with an explicit-target requirement instead of delivering to ambient DM / `@heartbeat`.
- What was not tested: Live Telegram heartbeat round-trip in a real workspace (CS acceptance criteria for this issue are unit/source-level; open PR #103660 is a weaker sentinel-only approach and was not used as base).

## AI disclosure

This fix was authored with AI assistance (Grok). Proof commands and results above were run on the local machine.

target.title: fix(terminal): strip no-argument C1 CSI sequences in sanitization
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`stripAnsiForSanitization` (used by `sanitizeForLog` and `sanitizeTerminalText`) only matched C1 CSI sequences that had at least one parameter or intermediate byte (`\x9b[\x20-\x3f]+[\x40-\x7e]`). No-argument C1 CSI sequences such as `\x9b@` (ICH), `\x9bA` (CUU), `\x9bB` (CUD), etc. were not recognized, so the C1 introducer was stripped as a control character while the final byte leaked into log/agent-visible output.

This is the same class of terminal escape leak fixed by #103672, but for C1 CSI rather than C1 OSC.

## Why This Change Was Made

Replaced `PARAMETERIZED_C1_ANSI_CSI_PATTERN` (which required `+` parameter bytes) with the existing `C1_ANSI_CSI_PATTERN` (which uses `*`) in `SANITIZATION_ANSI_SEQUENCE_REGEX`. This makes the sanitizer recognize complete C1 CSI sequences with or without parameters, while still preserving truly ambiguous lone `\x9b` bytes (those not followed by a final byte) for the control-character pass to remove.

Updated adjacent tests so that lone-C1-control cases do not accidentally form complete CSI sequences.

## User Impact

Log messages, error strings, and sanitized terminal text now correctly remove no-argument C1 CSI escape sequences instead of leaving stray final bytes in model/LLM-readable output.

## Real behavior proof

Negative control (origin/main version of `packages/terminal-core/src/ansi.ts`):

```text
\x9b@: stripAnsi=""  stripAnsiForSanitization="\x9b@"  sanitizeForLog="@"  <<< LEAK
\x9bA: stripAnsi=""  stripAnsiForSanitization="\x9bA"  sanitizeForLog="A"  <<< LEAK

## What Problem This Solves

`submitGeminiBatch()` reads the full error response body via `batchRes.text()`
on non-404 batch-create failures with no size limit.

## Why This Change Was Made

Replace the unbounded `batchRes.text()` with `createProviderHttpError()` — the
canonical bounded provider error helper — so error body consumption is capped
at 16 KiB and structured error metadata is preserved.

## User Impact

**Before:** unbounded error body read, potential memory exhaustion on large
error responses
**After:** bounded at 16 KiB via `createProviderHttpError`, 404 special case
preserved with actionable message

## Evidence

stream` drives `runGeminiEmbeddingBatches` — the exact production function that

## Summary

Fixes #53250.

When `host=node` exec approval is required but no approval UI is available, the exec approval unavailable path could still fall back to generic guidance:

`exec denied: approval required (approval UI not available)`

That tells the operator something is wrong, but not what to do next for a node-hosted command. This patch moves the recovery guidance into the shared exec approval unavailable renderer used by the current host=node exec path, then names two concrete recovery paths:
- open the Control UI with `openclaw dashboard --no-open`
- inspect pending approvals with `openclaw approvals get --node <id|name|ip>` or the resolved node id when available

## What Problem This Solves

The existing WhatsApp debounce setting is too broad for mixed usage.

Some conversations should be processed immediately, while others should wait briefly so OpenClaw can batch several short messages into one agent turn. This matters for owner chats, external direct chats, and busy groups that need different timing.

AI-assisted: yes, Codex helped update this branch and evidence.

## Why This Change Was Made

This adds per-conversation inbound debounce settings for WhatsApp direct chats and groups while keeping the existing channel-level debounce as the fallback.

The runtime now supports:

- `channels.whatsapp.direct["<id>"].debounceMs`

Examples:

- owner/admin direct chats can use `debounceMs: 0` for immediate turns

target.title: feat(config): support externally managed GitOps config
target.body:
Closes #103606

Related: #55753, #59616, #83851, #89526

Prior related PRs: #90653, #96438

## What Problem This Solves

Kubernetes and GitOps operators currently have to choose between mounting an
externally owned config as mutable local state or replacing the pod when a
ConfigMap generation changes. That makes safe config changes drop active
sessions and lets OpenClaw write back into a source whose desired state belongs
to Flux, Argo CD, Nix, or another controller.

## Why This Change Was Made

This adds a host-only `OPENCLAW_CONFIG_MANAGED=1` ownership contract: OpenClaw
continues to read and reconcile the config, but all config-writing CLI and
Gateway surfaces reject before side effects. The Gateway watches both the
configured path and its bounded parent, reconciles Kubernetes AtomicWriter
symlink swaps in process, and keeps its diff baseline at the last successfully
applied generation so failed, ignored, and restart-pending generations cannot
poison later reload decisions.

The Kubernetes example now mounts a stable, read-only ConfigMap directory at
`/etc/openclaw-config`, keeps runtime state on the PVC, and avoids a config hash
rollout trigger. Nix keeps its existing ownership/error contract. General
`$include` dependency watching and a transactional redesign of OpenClaw's own
internal config-write pipeline are intentionally out of scope; settings already
classified as restart-required still use the normal lifecycle restart path.

## User Impact

GitOps-managed pods can apply hot-safe root config changes without restarting
the pod, preserving active sessions and in-memory state. Operators get a clear,
consistent `OPENCLAW_CONFIG_MANAGED` error from setup, config, agent, skill, and
plugin mutation surfaces instead of a late filesystem failure. Invalid external
generations leave the last applied runtime active until the controller publishes
a valid replacement.

## Evidence

- AWS Crabbox `cbx_cace403c44f7` (released), exact rebased head:
  - `run_d7143581a688`: 1,095 focused assertions passed across 9 Vitest shards,
    including real AtomicWriter `..data` swaps and an out-of-parent symlink target.
  - `run_853f68350f67`: `pnpm check:changed` passed core/core-test typechecks,
    sharded lint, script lint, dependency/boundary guards, and import-cycle checks.
  - `run_8437bd887cb6`: production `pnpm build` passed.

target.title: fix(novita): discover live account model catalog for listing and runtime (#103532)
target.body:
## Summary

The Novita provider plugin only exposed its **static manifest catalog**, so `openclaw models list --provider novita` and runtime model resolution never saw account-available routes (e.g. the reported `novita/deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash`). This PR adds authenticated **live model discovery** — activated through the plugin manifest — with the static catalog kept as an offline/auth-failure fallback.

Fixes #103532.

## What Problem This Solves

After configuring a Novita API key, the model selector stayed empty and a configured model like `novita/deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash` failed at runtime with `Unknown model … no matching models.providers["novita"].models[]`. The shipped plugin returned only fixed manifest rows and never queried the account catalog.

## Root Cause

- `provider-catalog.ts` returned only the static `NOVITA_MODEL_CATALOG`.
- Provider-filtered listing returns manifest rows before consulting a live catalog, and the runtime unknown-model path rejects any model absent from the resolved catalog.
- **Critically**, the Novita manifest did not opt into live discovery, so `catalog.run` / `augmentModelCatalog` hooks stay inert in production (listing returns static rows before `catalog.run`; bundled loading skips `augmentModelCatalog` without `runtimeAugment`).

## Changes

- **`openclaw.plugin.json`**: declare `modelCatalog.runtimeAugment = true` and `discovery.novita = "refreshable"` so provider-filtered listing consults `catalog.run` and bundled loading runs `augmentModelCatalog` (mirrors `chutes` / `anthropic`).
- **`provider-catalog.ts`**: authenticated live discovery via the provider SDK cached live-catalog runtime (`getCachedLiveProviderModelRows`, SSRF-guarded, 5s timeout, 5min TTL). When discovery succeeds, **curated static metadata (reasoning, vision, context, pricing) is preserved for models the manifest already knows**, conservative synthesis is used only for new account-only routes. A custom Novita baseUrl suppresses discovery so the credential is never sent to the public endpoint.
- **`index.test.ts`**: regression coverage for manifest activation, live discovery reaching both listing and runtime-registration paths with a `Bearer` header, and known-vs-new metadata behavior.
- **`docs/providers/novita.md`**: clarify the bundled list is the offline fallback.

## Evidence

**CI:** all required checks green (types, lint, extension-package-boundary, extension-bundled, test shards).

**Credentialed live proof (real Novita API key, redacted `sk_***…*** (46 chars)`)** — driving the **real** `buildNovitaProvider` against the **real** `https://api.novita.ai/openai/v1/models` endpoint:

```
=== static fallback catalog ===
count: 6

=== LIVE account catalog (real Novita /models) ===
count: 139
discovery active (differs from static): true
includes reported model 'deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash': true
account-only routes not in static (sample): baidu/ernie-4.5-300b-a47b-paddle,
  baidu/ernie-4.5-vl-424b-a47b, deepseek/deepseek_v3, deepseek/deepseek-ocr, ...
known model kimi-k2.5 kept curated metadata:
  {"reasoning":true,"input":["text","image"],"contextWindow":262144}
```

This confirms provider-filtered listing surfaces account-only routes (incl. the reported `deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash`), and that curated metadata for known models survives the sparse live rows.

**Runtime turn:** a live chat completion returned `HTTP 403 {"reason":"NOT_ENOUGH_BALANCE"}` for every model (including known static routes) — the test account has no inference credit, so a completion cannot be demonstrated with this key. This is an account-balance limitation, not a code issue; the discovery/listing/registration path is fully exercised above.

## AI-assisted

Fixes an issue where backend clients retrying a failed `chat.send` with the same idempotency key could not tell that the Gateway had returned a stored result. A cached retryable error therefore looked fresh and could be resubmitted until the client's retry budget was exhausted.

## Why This Change Was Made

This replaces the broad metadata forwarding proposed in #98206 with a narrow negotiated contract:

- `response-replay` is an explicit client capability.
- The only wire metadata is the closed JSON shape `{ replayed: true }`.
- `RespondFn` keeps arbitrary diagnostic metadata in a separate log-only argument.
- Clients without the capability receive the unchanged strict response envelope.
- The official TypeScript Gateway client advertises the capability and exposes `GatewayClientRequestError.replayed`, providing an in-tree consumer.

`runId`, diagnostic `error`/`channel` values, and plugin metadata are never copied into the response metadata object.

## User Impact

Retrying clients can stop resubmitting the same idempotency key after the Gateway returns a stored retryable error. Existing clients and native apps that do not advertise `response-replay` see no new response-frame fields.

## Evidence

- Post-rebase focused run: 67 unit tests and 110 Gateway tests passed.
- Full TypeScript project graph passed: `node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -b tsconfig.projects.json`.
- Full build passed with the repository's no-pnpm fallback: `OPENCLAW_BUILD_ALL_NO_PNPM=1 node scripts/build-all.mjs`.
- Formatting passed for every changed TypeScript/Markdown file.
- Extensions and scripts lint shards passed; the changed Gateway responder passed targeted type-aware core lint.
- Protocol and Swift models were regenerated; `ResponseFrame.meta` remains optional with a default-`nil` Swift initializer parameter.
- Tests verify the strict schema rejects arbitrary/legacy metadata, legacy clients receive no `meta`, opted-in clients receive only `{ replayed: true }`, cached `chat.send` paths supply the dedicated wire argument, and the TypeScript client consumes it on request errors.

The live WebSocket capture in #98206 already established that the original responder path dropped metadata. This PR does not repeat that transport-only proof; it adds the consumer, negotiation, safety boundary, and client-consumption proof requested in the closing review.

target.title: Avoid full transcript parse during successor rotation
target.body:
## Draft Status

This draft is paused after a fresh correctness and performance review. The current head is not ready for maintainer review.

The sampled reader avoids materializing the full transcript, but its prefix safety scan still reads the old history linearly. On the current metric fixture it read `3,473,005` bytes for a `3,374,701`-byte transcript. On a same-shape 8.84 MB fixture, full rotation measured `45.603 ms` median and the sampled path measured `57.596 ms` (`26.3%` slower). The earlier `30%` speedup evidence is therefore no longer valid.

The review also found that message-only sibling branches and older compaction records can live entirely before the sampled tail. Preserving those semantics requires either scanning the prefix structure or having durable branch/carry-state metadata. Treating every prefix message as a fallback condition would remove the fast path.

## Problem

Issue #99190 tracks long-lived session transcripts whose JSONL files are read and parsed in full on hot paths. This draft explored one bounded slice: file-backed post-compaction successor rotation.

## Current Approach

- Read a small session-header window and recent tail.
- Align the tail to complete JSONL records.
- Use the sampled path only for the current transcript version.
- Scan older prefix rows for preservation-sensitive state and fall back to the full reader when the sample cannot prove equivalence.

## What Is Needed Before Resuming

- A durable index or checkpoint that proves branch and carry-state completeness without scanning the entire prefix, or an explicit decision to change inactive-branch preservation semantics.
- Exact-range reads that loop to completion or fall back on short reads.
- Sampled records normalized through the same canonical loader as the full reader.
- A strict differential evaluator covering message-only sibling branches, older compactions, legacy content normalization, malformed rows, short reads, and very large individual records.
- Fresh end-to-end timing and byte-read evidence after all correctness gates pass.

The existing focused suite on the draft head passed, but it does not establish the missing prefix completeness or a performance win.

Related to #99190

target.title: fix(agents): preserve ANSI sanitizer state across bash chunks

Closes #103668

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users running bash commands through agents could see ANSI/OSC control-sequence fragments leak into streamed tool output, final bash results, and full-output spill files when a process split a terminal sequence across output callbacks.

## Why This Change Was Made

The fix adds a reusable incremental ANSI sequence stripper in terminal-core and lets the bash output accumulator use one sanitizer instance for the lifetime of each command. This preserves streaming and bounded-memory behavior while keeping one-shot `stripAnsiSequences()` semantics unchanged for existing callers.

## User Impact

target.title: fix(discord): retry reply session init conflicts to prevent silent message loss
target.body:
Closes #102381

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Discord inbound messages could be silently dropped when a reply session initialization conflict (`reply session initialization conflicted for <sessionKey>`) raced with another turn finishing or another event initializing the same session. Telegram, Signal, and Slack already retry this transient condition; Discord did not, so the user saw no reply and the message was lost.

## Why This Change Was Made

Added bounded exponential backoff retry inside `processDiscordMessageInner` (`extensions/discord/src/monitor/message-handler.process.ts`) to match the existing Telegram callback-submit pattern and Slack/Signal retry semantics. The retry only applies to the specific reply-session-init-conflict error string; all other errors fail fast on the first attempt. If the run is aborted while retrying, the loop stops cleanly and returns without throwing.

**ClawSweeper review follow-up:** the retry boundary was narrowed so context/history preparation runs exactly once and only the dispatch/session-init attempt is retried. This prevents a Discord room event from being recorded twice when a conflict happens.

## User Impact

Discord users are far less likely to see a missing reply after sending a message that races with a session teardown or concurrent turn. Operators no longer need to ask the user to re-send; the retry covers the brief window where the session store CAS conflict occurs.

## Evidence

- Added a focused regression test suite in `extensions/discord/src/monitor/message-handler.process.test.ts`:
  - retries with exponential backoff until dispatch succeeds (250 ms, 1000 ms, 2500 ms)
  - throws the last error after exhausting retries
  - does not retry unrelated dispatch errors
  - stops retrying when the abort signal fires
  - **records room event history exactly once across conflict retries** (new regression test for the narrowed boundary)

target.title: fix(agents): lease session worktrees during runs
target.body:
## Summary

Session-backed managed worktrees are now leased and Git-locked for the lifetime of every agent run. Idle GC and a separate non-force remover both reject an admitted run's checkout, including when the run uses a subdirectory inside the worktree.

## Root cause

GC's owner-activity read and `git worktree remove --force` were independent operations. The previous patch repeated the read closer to removal, but a session could still be admitted after that read and while the destructive command started.

## Fix

The managed-worktree service now owns a per-worktree FIFO lease. `agent-command` acquires the lease before a session run touches its configured cwd and releases it in its outer cleanup. The lease retains the existing PID-tagged Git worktree lock, with local reference counting so only the final local holder unlocks it. All managed removal paths acquire the same queue through snapshotting and git removal; idle GC retains the owner-active guard after it has obtained that lease.

Lease lookup accepts a managed worktree root or one of its subdirectories, matching session worktrees whose configured workspace is nested below the repository root.

## Why this is the right boundary

The worktree service owns both the existing cross-process Git lock and destructive removal, so the same lifecycle primitive protects local and separate-service callers. Agent command is the session-run admission point that has the resolved cwd and can retain ownership through the actual runtime. Explicit removal keeps its existing force semantics, while an agent that loses the race before admission fails before using a deleted cwd rather than running against it.

## Verification

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/worktrees/service.test.ts`: 25 passed.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/command/worktree-lease.test.ts`: passed.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/gateway/server.sessions.create.test.ts src/gateway/server.sessions.delete-lifecycle.test.ts`: passed.
- `oxlint` and `oxfmt --check` on `src/agents/agent-command.ts`, `src/agents/worktrees/service.ts`, and `src/agents/worktrees/service.test.ts`: clean.
- `node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p tsconfig.core.json --incremental --tsBuildInfoFile .artifacts/tsgo-cache/worktree-gc-core.tsbuildinfo`: clean.

## Summary

- add experimental `claws status [claw-or-agent]` for installed-agent, workspace-file, partial-state, and package-reference visibility
- add read-only `claws remove <claw-or-agent> --dry-run --json` planning

This is the status/remove slice for the grouped one-Claw/one-agent contract. Package names may resolve an install when unambiguous; final agent ids are always accepted and are required when the same package has created multiple agents.

target.title: fix(skills): enforce 256 MiB skill download cap in-stream
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`downloadFile()` streams response body to disk via `pipeline()` without a byte
limit. A hostile server can send unbounded data, exhausting disk space.

## Why This Change Was Made

Added `SKILL_DOWNLOAD_MAX_BYTES` (100 MiB) enforced via a Transform stream
counter inside the pipeline. The stream is aborted as soon as the byte limit
is exceeded — before excess bytes reach disk. The existing `finally` block
cleans up the temp file and releases the guarded response.

## User Impact

**Before:** no limit — disk exhaustion possible
**After:** 100 MiB enforced in-stream, excess bytes never reach disk, staging
tmp file is removed, and guarded response is released.

## Evidence

Branch: `fix/install-download-maxbytes` | Base: `upstream/main` | Node: v22.19.0 — linux

### Real behavior proof

Two regression tests drive the real production `installDownloadSpec` entry point
(the exact function called by the skill installer). The HTTP layer is mocked
but the full production download pipeline — Transform counter, file write,
staging cleanup, and response release — executes exactly as it does in production.

**Test 1 — oversized download aborted mid-stream (> 100 MiB):**
- A streaming body emits 64 KiB chunks until the counter exceeds 100 MiB
- The Transform counter calls `file.destroy(err)` and `callback(err)`
- `pipeline()` stops forwarding chunks, the stream is destroyed
- Staging `.tmp` file is cleaned up by the `finally` block
- Guarded `release()` is called

**Test 2 — small download completes normally (4 KiB):**
- A 4 KiB body passes through the counter without hitting the limit
- The download completes without any size-limit error
- Guarded `release()` is called

### Regression tests

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/skills/lifecycle/install-download.test.ts --reporter=verbose

target.title: fix(cron): persist startup catch-up deferrals
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes #102236. A startup overflow catch-up slot could be persisted to SQLite while its protection marker existed only in memory. Restarting again before that slot fired let maintenance advance the job to its next natural cron slot, silently losing the deferred run.

## Why This Change Was Made

The deferral marker now lives on `CronJobState` as `pendingCatchupDeferral`, so the existing `state_json` persistence and rollback paths own the slot and marker together. The process-local Set and its parallel rollback bookkeeping are removed. Maintenance clears the persisted marker when the slot arrives, when no valid deferred slot remains, or when the job is disabled; execution also clears it after an outcome. Existing rows need no migration because an absent field means no pending deferral.

## User Impact

Overflow system-event cron jobs keep their staggered startup catch-up run across repeated gateway restarts instead of silently skipping to the next natural schedule. Unrelated stale future cron slots are still repaired normally.

## Evidence

- Real SQLite restart path: one service starts and persists an overflow deferral, a fresh service starts 3 seconds later against the same store, the original 5-second slot survives, executes once, and clears its marker.

target.title: fix: strip volatile output from exec result hash to fix no-progress detection (#93917)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where repeated failed `exec` calls never triggered the no-progress
circuit breaker when the error output text varied across calls. This happens
commonly with command-not-found, timeouts, and killed processes whose error
message carries fresh timestamps, PIDs, or session ids each retry while the
actual failure mode is identical.

Fixes #93917

## Why This Change Was Made

`hashExecToolOutcome` is split so a `failed` exec result is hashed without its
volatile output text, while a `completed` result keeps output in the hash as a
real progress signal. Failed retries are instead compared by stable failure
metadata (`status`, `exitCode`, `timedOut`, `exitSignal`, `failureKind`), so
identical failures with different error strings still count as no progress.

The production foreground exec path now carries those stable discriminators end
to end: `ExecToolDetails` (and `buildExecForegroundResult` plus the node-host and
gateway producers) propagate `failureKind` and `exitSignal`, tightened to
`ExecToolFailureKind`, so the hash receives real values at runtime instead of
`null`. This addresses @vincentkoc's blocking finding that the discriminators
were absent on the real result.

## User Impact

Stuck agents that loop retrying the same failed `exec` call now correctly hit the
global circuit breaker after the configured threshold, stopping runaway sessions
instead of burning tokens forever. Genuinely different failure modes stay
distinct and are not merged.

## Changes

| File | Change |
|------|--------|
| `bash-tools.exec-types.ts` | Add `ExecToolFailureKind`; `failed` `ExecToolDetails` carries `exitSignal` + `failureKind` |
| `bash-tools.exec-host-node-phases.ts`, `bash-tools.exec-runtime.ts`, `bash-tools.exec-host-gateway.ts` | Propagate stable failure fields through the real foreground producers |
| `tool-loop-detection.ts` | Split `hashExecToolOutcome`: `completed` keeps output; `failed` strips output, keeps `{status,exitCode,timedOut,exitSignal,failureKind}` |
| `tool-loop-detection.exec-foreground.test.ts` | **Real foreground exec** regression test through the production tool path |
| `tool-loop-detection.test.ts` | Unit coverage for failure-kind / exitSignal distinctness |
| `docs/tools/loop-detection.md` | Document the completed-vs-failed outcome equivalence rule |

## Evidence

### Real foreground exec proof (production tool path, no hand-built details)

`tool-loop-detection.exec-foreground.test.ts` drives the actual exec tool
(`createOpenClawCodingTools` -> `execTool.execute`) against a command that fails
with volatile stderr but identical params, then feeds each real result through
the production recorders (`recordToolCall` / `recordToolCallOutcome`) and
`detectToolCallLoop`.

The real foreground failed result (captured at exact head) carries the stable
discriminators — not manufactured values:

```
first failed details: {"status":"failed","exitCode":127,"exitSignal":null,"failureKind":"shell-command-not-found"}
breaker: {"stuck":true,"level":"critical","detector":"global_circuit_breaker","count":4,
          "warningKey":"global:exec:...:bed082ca..."}   # identical outcome hash across 4 varying-stderr calls
distinct: {"notFound":"shell-command-not-found","notFoundExit":127,
           "timedOut":"overall-timeout","timedOutSignal":"SIGTERM"}
```

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/tool-loop-detection.exec-foreground.test.ts
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  2 passed (2)
```

- A real `status:"failed"` foreground exec result carries `failureKind` +
  `exitSignal` into the hash (runtime contract, not unit-only).
- Repeated identical failures with varying stderr trip `global_circuit_breaker`.
- Two genuinely different real failure modes (`shell-command-not-found` vs
  `overall-timeout`) keep distinct fingerprints and do not merge.

### Mutation proof — the fix is what trips the breaker

Reverting only the `failed` branch of `hashExecToolOutcome` to include the
volatile output text (the pre-fix behavior) makes the same real-foreground test
fail, because varying stderr yields a fresh hash each call so the streak never
accumulates:

```
 × trips the no-progress breaker on repeated failed exec with volatile stderr
 AssertionError: expected undefined to be 'global_circuit_breaker'
```

Restoring the fix returns the test to green.

### Unit + regression suites

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/tool-loop-detection.test.ts src/agents/tool-loop-detection.exec-foreground.test.ts
 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  60 passed (60)
```

### Maintainer decision still needed

This intentionally changes when failed retries count as no progress (stable
failure metadata now outweighs varying error text). Whether repeated failed exec
with the same stable fingerprint should trip critical/global blocking is a policy
call owned by the assigned reviewer (@vincentkoc). The code, docs, and
exact-head real-foreground proof are in place for that decision.

The Nostr outbound adapter (`extensions/nostr/src/gateway.ts:nostrOutboundAdapter`) had no `sanitizeText` hook. ## Why This Change Was Made

- **Root cause:** the outbound adapter omits the `sanitizeText` hook that strips internal runtime scaffolding before delivery, and the adapter's narrowed `Pick` type did not even include the field.

## User Impact

Internal tool-trace banners and leaked XML scaffolding no longer reach Nostr DM recipients. Ordinary assistant prose is preserved unchanged.

N/A (no existing issue). Sibling fixes: #103109, #98693, #98705.

## Evidence

Terminal capture of `node --import tsx` runtime verification calling the **patched adapter hook** `nostrOutboundAdapter.sanitizeText` (exact hook added by this PR) on the exact PR head:

target.title: fix: prevent operational notices from leaking to source chats
target.body:
<details>
<summary>Additional instructions</summary>

**MUST:** Keep **Allow edits from maintainers** enabled for this PR so maintainers can help update the branch when needed.

</details>

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users interacting with agents through external chats such as WhatsApp could see automatic runtime notices when model fallback, usage limits, compaction, backend failures, heartbeat checks, ACP status, plugin-binding failures, or tool/progress warnings happened.

## Why This Change Was Made

This adds `messages.operationalReplies` so operators can control automatic operational notices separately from normal assistant replies. The policy supports `always`, `silent`, `once`, and `redirect`; `redirect` writes notices to an operator session through `redirectSessionKey`, and `sendPolicy: deny` still wins.

The policy is applied across direct dispatch, ACP delivery, ACP status projection, queued follow-ups, compaction notices, route-failure notices, heartbeat delivery, progress/status callbacks, plugin-binding notices, tool warnings, and block/final replies. Normal message-tool replies, authorized command replies, before-run block replies, and background ACP child suppression keep their existing behavior.

The branch was rebased on current `origin/main`. Redirect-failure behavior uses the maintainer-selected fail-closed contract: if the configured operator redirect write fails, the source chat remains suppressed and the failure is logged instead of exposing operational details back to the source chat.

A follow-up review found plain `isError` payloads were too broad to classify as operational notices. This branch now treats only explicit notice flags or internal notice metadata as operational, and it keeps normal error replies visible under `messages.operationalReplies`.

AI-assisted: yes, Codex helped update this branch and evidence.

## User Impact

Operators can keep fallback, usage-limit, backend-error, compaction, heartbeat, status, ACP, follow-up, plugin-binding, and tool-warning notices out of external chats while still preserving logs or redirecting those notices to an operator-owned session. Existing configs keep current behavior because the default policy is `always`.

## Evidence

### Real Behavior Proof: WhatsApp-like Source Chat

Earlier redacted terminal proof on this branch used the actual `applyOperationalReplyPolicy` helper, a real temp `sessions.json`, and a source context shaped like an external WhatsApp direct chat:

This proves the affected external-source path does not deliver the operational fallback/error notice back to the source chat under `silent`, and under `redirect` it keeps source chat sends at zero while writing the notice, source session, source channel, and notice kind into the configured operator session transcript.

target.title: fix(discord): keep code fences intact when rebalancing reasoning italics
target.body:
Closes #102911

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Discord reasoning messages that wrap content in `_…_` would corrupt markdown code fences and inline code when the message was split across chunks. After a chunk boundary that started with a code delimiter, the italics rebalancer could prepend `_` (breaking `_```python` / `_~~~` / `_`code``) or leave unmatched trailing `_` on continuation chunks.

## Why This Change Was Made

`rebalanceReasoningItalics` still closes/reopens reasoning italics so each Discord message stays independently balanced. When the next chunk starts with a code delimiter:

1. Do **not** prepend `_` onto the code opener.
2. Reopen italics **after** the leading fenced or inline code span when later reasoning text continues.
3. Drop a lone trailing `_` on pure-code continuations.
4. Only append a closing `_` when the chunk actually opened reasoning italics.

The leading code-span scanner reuses the chunker’s fence grammar (`FENCE_RE` / `parseFenceLine`):

- backtick **or tilde** fences (` ``` ` / `~~~`)
- optional **0–3 space** indent
- **longer** closing markers (same char, length ≥ open)

Regression tests assert exact second-chunk output and even `_` counts for backtick, tilde, indented, longer-close, inline, and pure-code cases.

## User Impact

Discord reasoning/thinking replies that contain code blocks or inline code no longer break markdown fences at chunk boundaries, including tilde and indented fences, and each chunk keeps balanced reasoning italics when text continues after code.

## Evidence

### Focused tests
```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/discord/src/chunk.test.ts

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  24 passed (24)
```

### Production-path harness (`chunkDiscordText` → `rebalanceReasoningItalics`)

**Current main (before):** second chunk could start with `_```python…` (broken fence).

**This patch (exact second chunks):**
```
tilde:      "~~~python\nprint(1)\n~~~\n_more_"
indent:     "  ```python\nprint(1)\n  ```\n_more_"
long-close: "```python\nprint(1)\n````\n_more_"
```
All chunks have even `_` counts; openers are not prefixed with `_`.

### Changed-lane gates
```
OPENCLAW_CHECK_CHANGED_REMOTE_CHILD=1 CI=1 node scripts/check-changed.mjs  # PASS
pnpm test:changed  # PASS (extensions/discord/src/chunk.test.ts, 24 tests)
```

## Real behavior proof

- Behavior addressed: Discord reasoning-italics rebalance protects code-leading openers using the full chunker fence grammar and keeps per-message `_` balance.
- Environment: local macOS, OpenClaw checkout, Node 24; production helper `chunkDiscordText`. Verification host: local macOS (Crabbox bypass).
- Current-main contrast: with `maxLines: 10`, a reasoning body whose continuation starts at a fenced block produced `_```…` on main; incomplete parsers also missed tilde / indented / longer-close forms.
- Exact steps or command run after this patch:
  1. `node --import tsx` harness for tilde, indented, and longer-close fixtures
  2. `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/discord/src/chunk.test.ts`
  3. `OPENCLAW_CHECK_CHANGED_REMOTE_CHILD=1 CI=1 node scripts/check-changed.mjs`
  4. `pnpm test:changed`
- Evidence after fix: exact second-chunk outputs above; 24/24 tests green including tilde, indented, longer-close, inline, and pure-code cases.
- Control check: normal multi-chunk reasoning still reopens with leading `_` on non-code continuations.
- Observed result after fix: supported fence forms stay intact and each emitted message remains delimiter-balanced.
- What was not tested: live Discord API delivery in a real workspace (source-level path is the production chunker used before send).

## AI disclosure

This fix was authored with AI assistance (Grok). Implementation, tests, and proof were verified against ClawSweeper review findings on #103166 (balance code-leading chunks; reuse full fence grammar).

target.title: feat(channels): add typed cross-surface approval actions
target.body:
Related: #103505

Stacked on #103579. Review this branch from `codex/durable-approval-registry`.

## What Problem This Solves

Approval controls in chat currently encode product semantics as slash-command strings or infer the approval owner from an ID prefix. Long IDs can exceed transport callback limits, and a click on one surface can report the attempted decision instead of the canonical result already chosen elsewhere.

## Why This Change Was Made

This adds an explicit approval action to the portable presentation contract, a fixed-size durable resolution reference for constrained callbacks, and kind-aware canonical resolution across bundled approval channels. URL and Web App actions are typed at the same boundary; shipped command and legacy button inputs remain deprecated compatibility paths.

Channel plugins remain transport-only: core supplies the approval ID, owner kind, and decision; Telegram, Discord, Slack, Google Chat, Matrix, QQ, iMessage, Signal, and WhatsApp encode only private transport locators and render the canonical first-answer result. Durable cross-message terminal reconciliation is intentionally deferred to the later lifecycle stack described in `docs/refactor/operator-approvals.md`.

The canonical resolver responds with committed SQLite truth before detached channel, push, and legacy-event follow-up. Slow or failed secondary delivery therefore cannot delay the winning surface or hide the recorded result.

## User Impact

Operators can answer the same pending approval from supported chat surfaces without approval-ID truncation or owner inference. Concurrent answers converge on the SQLite-backed first answer, and the clicked surface shows that canonical terminal outcome even when another surface won.

## Evidence

- Focused iMessage shared-forwarding matrix: 101/101 tests passed, including numeric ROWID to exact tapback GUID correlation and strict typed binding checks.
- Focused channel suites: Telegram 144, Discord 39, Feishu 64, Slack 107, Google Chat 14, Matrix 25, WhatsApp 17, plus Signal and QQ approval regressions passed.
- Protocol generation/check: 63 tests passed; generated Swift models are current.
- Plugin SDK contracts: export sync, API baseline, surface ceilings, subpath imports, and runtime side-effect guards passed.
- A slow-forwarder regression proves `approval.resolve` returns the committed CAS result before best-effort fanout completes.
- Full Testbox changed gate passed after the Telegram regression fix: typecheck 126.39s, lint 53.01s, import cycles 4.11s, and every structural/storage/dependency guard green ([run](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29088376751)).

target.title: feat(ui): add standalone operator approval links
target.body:
Related: #103505

Stacked on #103679. Review this branch from `codex/approval-typed-actions`.

## What Problem This Solves

Approval prompts currently require the operator to remain on the surface that raised them. Even after the durable approval registry and typed channel actions, OpenClaw has no stable, mobile-friendly document that can be opened directly and refreshed to recover canonical approval state.

## Why This Change Was Made

This adds a standalone authenticated `${controlUiBasePath}/approve/{approvalId}` Control UI document backed by `approval.get` and `approval.resolve`. The Gateway reserves the one-segment approval namespace before plugins and static-file heuristics, including asset-like IDs, and fails closed with 404 when Control UI serving is disabled.

The document is bound to the Gateway that served it. It does not copy or overwrite the full app's saved remote-Gateway selection; URL/session authentication remains ephemeral until an operator explicitly confirms a different Gateway. Approval IDs are decoded once, credentials never enter the approval URL, and terminal state always comes from the SQLite-backed canonical record.

Resolution returns committed SQLite truth before best-effort channel, push, and legacy-event follow-up. A slow or failed secondary surface therefore cannot delay the winning response or replace its result.

## User Impact

Operators can open a stable approval link on a phone or desktop, authenticate, inspect the sanitized command or plugin preview, and approve or deny. Concurrent answers show `Approved here` on the winner and `Resolved elsewhere` with the recorded canonical decision on losers. Reload, reconnect, expiry, cancellation, malformed data, and unavailable approvals all fail closed without usable decision controls.

## Evidence

- Source-blind built-UI behavior validation passed all 9/9 contract clauses: standalone routing, mounted authentication, exact ID/kind/decision submission, first-answer winner and loser states, terminal reload, fail-closed malformed data, reconnect recovery, dynamic content, 48px mobile targets, no horizontal overflow, and zero browser page/console errors.
